content:
I didn't see any details of your pipeline. Is it verified?

With https://peregrine-project.github.io/ we can generate a number of these languages in a verified way.

Fair question, I think we target different use cases. No, lungo's pipeline isn't independently verified. It feeds off of Lean's own compiler IR and replaces Lean's runtime with a more portable implementation, and the result is checked against Lean's native backend, so it's tested rather than proven.
Peregrine has an intermediate language that it translates into and generates code from (based on my cursory reading, so correct me). lungo doesn't concern itself with redoing what the Lean compiler already does. In fact one could say lungo's intermediate language is Lean's own IR. lungo is focused on bridging proven Lean code into application programming languages.
Our Peregrine project takes Lean code and translates it to many languages, in a verified way. Lungo looks like a tested, but not verified, variant of this, IIUC.

lungo isn't a variant of Peregrine. It's a different philosophy. Peregrine sets out to unify proof assistants behind one intermediate language, so it has to re-derive what a Lean program means from its kernel terms. lungo doesn't. It makes Lean the source of truth for application code, so it starts from what Lean's own compiler produces and runs exactly what Lean runs: primitives, IO, Tasks, the whole standard library. Its output is checked byte for byte against Lean's native backend.
By your own docs, the Lean frontend is only "partially verified" and doesn't support primitives, IO or Tasks. The verified backends are C, Wasm, OCaml and CakeML; Rust is unverified, and Go, Python, TypeScript and Swift aren't targets. So "takes Lean code and translates it to many languages, in a verified way" isn't true for Lean today.
lungo is tested, not verified, and for what it's built for that's the right trade: proven Lean code, running unchanged in the languages applications are actually written in.
4 messages were moved here from #Project announcements > Treating Lean code as spec, and generating code based on it by Kevin Buzzard.

Peregrine restricts to functional code and includes primitives. Adding IO would be possible, I think, but we haven't done so yet.
Our F* collaborators have started to look at that.

Meanwhile, we have verified part of the front-end, the missing parts are mostly limitations of lean4lean, that we are contributing too.

Rust is unverified because there is no full formal semantics of the language. Compilation to rust mostly uses the verified pipeline, the final part, printing to rust is unverified. It may be possible to do something similar for the other languages you mention, but I haven't tried.

Thanks, that clarifies the frontend and Rust. The restriction to functional code makes sense for Peregrine, an intermediate language shared by proof assistants with very different ecosystems has to stick to what they have in common. lungo goes the other way. It takes Lean as it actually executes, with primitives, IO and Tasks, whose meaning Lean's compiler and runtime define, and carries that into application languages unchanged. Different goals, so a different trade between proving the pipeline and covering the language.

Really appreciate you taking the time to look at this, I learned a lot from this conversation and it means a lot to have caught your attention. I'll be following Peregrine closely, especially the Lean frontend.
